research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require an irreducibly agent-relative mode of representation, or can a rigid third-personal representation of an agent's intention and act suffice?

argument.title: Self-Location Constraint
argument.paper_title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience

premises.text: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about one outcome rather than another, its cognition must represent the first outcome as its own action.
premises.quote: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about φ rather than ψ, then the agent’s cognitive state must represent φ as the outcome of its own action rather than ψ.

premises.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents an outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than relevant alternatives.
premises.quote: where responsibility is understood contrastively, the cognitive state constitutive of responsible agency must itself represent the relevant outcome as issuing from the agent’s own activity rather than the relevant alternatives.

premises.text: A third-personal proposition identifying God as actualising a world does not itself represent that actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.
premises.quote: A third-personal proposition such as “God actualises W1” may identify the correct agent extensionally, yet it does not by itself represent the actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.

premises.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires divine cognition to represent God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.
premises.quote: The relevant question is not merely which world becomes actual, but whether divine cognition represents God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.

missing_premise.text: God's contrastive responsibility for actualising one world rather than another is robust responsibility, and representing God as the source of that actualisation requires irreducible de se content.

conclusion.text: If God is contrastively responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include irreducible de se content.

challenged_premise.text: A third-personal proposition identifying God as actualising a world does not itself represent that actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.

objection: God’s cognition uses only a rigid identifier, “G,” for the unique being whose intentions directly control which world becomes actual. G considers W0 and W1, judges W1 better, forms the intention expressed as “G will actualise W1,” and W1 consequently becomes actual. G then knows the proposition “G actualised W1 rather than W0 because G intended W1.” The identifier is third-personal: it carries no first-personal mode of presentation. Yet the proposition identifies the source perfectly. It singles out the unique controller, connects that being’s intention to the resulting world, and excludes every alternative source. Nothing further supplied by “I actualised W1” would improve the attribution of the actualisation to G.

strongest_responses.response: The G-proposition identifies the controller and connects G's intention to W1, but robust responsibility requires representing the outcome as the agent's own doing, not merely as a causally explained event involving that agent. A rigid designator fixes reference without fixing the agent's stance toward the act.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The objector's example already represents W1 as issuing from G's intention and control. Defender A conceded that the argument did not independently show why the further agent-relative stance matters for responsibility.

strongest_responses.response: The argument should distinguish third-personal source-identifying content from practically self-ascriptive cognition that represents actualisation as issuing from that very agent's agency. The relevant condition concerns intentional agency rather than the grammatical form of a proposition.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: This reformulation preserves a possible route to the conclusion, but it revises rather than establishes c008. It leaves open whether the G-thought can itself have the required practical role despite its third-personal form.

closest_literature.title: Baysüngür Philosophical Views: Timeless Divine Knowledge, Human Freedom, and the Experience–Choice Cycle

nearest.title: Baysüngür Philosophical Views: Timeless Divine Knowledge, Human Freedom, and the Experience–Choice Cycle

open_questions: What responsibility-relevant difference, if any, separates knowing that G intentionally actualised W1 from representing that actualisation under an agent-relative aspect?
Can a thought expressed with a rigid third-personal identifier be practically self-ascriptive for its bearer?
Must agent-relative representation involve irreducible de se content, or can its role in intention and control supply the relevant self-ascription?
What account of robust contrastive responsibility establishes that a stance of doing is necessary in addition to accurate source identification and intentional control?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the argument from divine contrastive responsibility to irreducible de se content depends on a substantive agency condition, not on the merely third-personal grammar or referential precision of divine cognition. It would develop the distinction between source-identifying knowledge and practically self-ascriptive representation, anticipate the rigid-identifier case in which G's intention selects and produces W1, and show either that this case lacks the agency-relative aspect required for robust responsibility or that no such additional aspect is needed. To succeed, the paper would need to state and defend a responsibility-relevant criterion that distinguishes treating an intentional act as an object of knowledge from representing it as one's own doing.

reasons.coherence: The objection is internally consistent and correctly targets the 'required for source attribution' clause of c008, though c008's literal claim that third-personal content lacks a first-personal aspect is trivially true, so the real target needs to be stated more sharply.
reasons.robustness: The obvious reply is that intention-formation itself requires self-ascription, so the G-case presupposes de se uptake. The direction only lists this as an open question and does not answer it; Defender B's reformulation concedes the point rather than meeting it.
reasons.significance: If successful it would usefully show that the de se argument for divine omniscience depends on a contested agency condition, but this largely transposes an existing debate rather than reshaping discussion of this argument.
reasons.specificity: The proposal names a distinction and a test case, but its thesis is disjunctive ('show either that... or that...') and it gives no definite criterion or argumentative plan.

assessment.strongest_objection: The rigid-identifier case assumes the very thing it means to dispense with. For G to form 'the intention expressed as "G will actualise W1"' and for that intention to control which world becomes actual, G must take G to be itself. This is the Perry/Castañeda point about the messy shopper: someone can know 'the unique controller will actualise W1' without that knowledge engaging their agency. So the case either covertly includes de se self-ascription, or it describes a being that merely knows a fact about a controller and is not the agent. A referee would also note that the paper's real question (whether practical self-ascription needs irreducible de se content) is the existing essential-indexical debate (Perry, Lewis, Millikan, Cappelen & Dever's 'The Inessential Indexical', Magidor, Torre). The proposal neither engages that debate nor says what the divine case adds to it.
assessment.what_it_needs: It must commit to one horn and defend it against the essential-indexical literature. For example, it could argue in Cappelen–Dever style that the G-intention's functional role in control suffices without irreducible de se content. It must also explain why the divine case (no ignorance of identity, a single possible controller) changes the dialectic rather than just restating the messy-shopper debate.
assessment.summary: There is a real issue here, but as framed it reruns the essential-indexical debate without engaging it and dodges the obvious reply that forming G's intention already requires de se self-ascription; pick a side, engage Perry and Cappelen–Dever, and say what is distinctive about the divine case.

revision.research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility for actualising one world rather than another require irreducibly de se content in divine cognition, or can a rigid, de re representation of an agent's controlling intention and its act suffice when the agent's identity is not in doubt?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the inference from divine contrastive responsibility to irreducible de se content fails, because robust responsibility requires only that the agent's intention be the operative control state for the outcome, and that a rigid, de re representation of that intention satisfies this requirement. The paper would defend the Cappelen-Dever style horn: the functional role of G's intention in selecting and producing W1 is sufficient for source attribution, so no irreducible first-personal mode of presentation is needed. It would make two moves. First, it would concede the referee's strongest point, that forming an intention to actualise W1 involves practical self-ascription, and then distinguish two things that point runs together: practical self-ascription as a feature of the control state (G's intention is G's, and G knows that G is the being whose intention is operative), which is de re and identity-preserving, and de se content as an irreducible mode of presentation that the attribution needs in order to be correct. Second, it would argue that the divine case changes the dialectic in a specific way. In the messy-shopper cases the case for de se content rests on an epistemic gap about who one is, and that gap is absent here, since G has no ignorance of identity and there is only one possible controller. Holding identity knowledge fixed therefore isolates the agency condition itself. The paper would then argue that any remaining case for irreducible de se content must rest on that condition alone, and that the condition is satisfied by the rigid case without residue. The paper would not claim that c008's literal claim is informative. Its target is the 'required for source attribution' clause, which the paper would restate as a claim about what robust responsibility minimally requires.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The paper accepts the referee's premise that intention-formation involves self-ascription, and denies that this yields irreducible de se content. It draws the distinction between de re self-ascription, where the agent's identity with the controlling being is known under a rigid identifier and the intention is recognised as the operative control state, and de se content, where the proposition is individuated by a first-personal mode of presentation that cannot be replaced by a rigid one. The argument is that robust contrastive responsibility needs only the first. In the G-case the functional role of the intention in selecting and producing W1 supplies the agency condition, and the identity knowledge is trivial because G has no candidate for being someone else. The referee's messy-shopper contrast therefore does not carry over: its force depends on an identity gap, which the divine case lacks. The reply concedes that the referee's dilemma holds for any case with an identity gap, and argues that the divine case is not one.
revision.what_changed: The disjunctive thesis is replaced by a single committed claim: robust contrastive responsibility is satisfied by de re practical self-ascription, so irreducible de se content is not needed, and the divine case is used to isolate the agency condition by removing any identity gap.

reasons.coherence: It correctly targets the 'required for source attribution' clause of c008 and draws a distinction that makes sense, but there is a tension between conceding practical self-ascription in intention-formation and treating that self-ascription as purely de re, and the paper does not resolve it.
reasons.robustness: The no-identity-gap reply assumes that G's knowledge of being the unique controller can be had third-personally, which is exactly the point in dispute, and neither the plan nor the transcript answers the standard Lewis/Perry rejoinder.
reasons.significance: If it succeeded, it would block a recent argument that omniscience or divine agency requires irreducible de se content and would give anti-essential-indexical views a useful test case, but the result is a refinement within an established debate.
reasons.specificity: It has a definite thesis, a central case (the G-intention), and two stated moves, but it lacks the positive account of robust responsibility that its own fourth open question shows it needs.

assessment.strongest_objection: The paper's key move, that the divine case has no identity gap because G cannot be ignorant of who it is and there is only one possible controller, begs the question. Lewis's two-omniscient-gods case shows that knowing every third-personal proposition, including that a unique being G controls actualisation, does not fix which being one is. What closes that gap is self-locating knowledge. So 'G knows that G is the being whose intention is operative' is either the trivial de re truth G=G, which does no work, or it quietly relies on the de se content the paper denies. The Perry–Castañeda point also concerns how a thought connects to action, not only resolving ignorance. Removing the shopper's epistemic gap therefore does not isolate an agency condition that de re content can meet.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must show how a G-thought can be the operative, action-guiding state for its bearer without a self-locating link. This means engaging Lewis's two-gods case and the Cappelen-Dever versus Perry/Recanati/García-Carpintero literature directly. It must also give a positive account of robust contrastive responsibility on which intentional control plus de re source identification is sufficient. Relevant work on omniscience and indexicals (Grim, Kvanvig, Torre, Nagasawa) should be engaged, not the unrelated works listed.
assessment.summary: There is a paper-shaped idea here, but its central claim that the divine case lacks an identity gap assumes the point at issue, and it would not survive a referee who knows Lewis's two-gods case until it shows how third-personal intention can guide action without self-location.
